metric_rationale: The design contains four trial types (T7-T10) on which the two options split feature-wise wins exactly evenly (1-1 or 2-2), so the Tallying softmax is mathematically uniform for ANY beta and epsilon: Tallying must choose the highest-validity-cue winner exactly 50% of the time, with only binomial noise (32 such trials per subject => between-subject SD ~0.09). Take The Best, in contrast, resolves these pairs on the first discriminating cue and therefore chooses the top-cue winner with probability (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, which for essentially the whole plausible parameter range sits well above chance (~0.80-0.95). The metric is the proportion of tally-tie trials on which the option favored by the highest-validity discriminating cue was chosen. It is parameter-free for Tallying (fixed at 0.5, tight across subjects) and clearly above 0.5 for TTB, giving a large mean gap with modest per-subject variability. It also works identically on a single subject's slice and on the pooled data, and side/direction counterbalancing in the design ensures response bias cannot inflate it.

The design contains conflict trials in which the tally winner and the one-reason (TTB) winner are opposite options, and where the tally margin is large (|M| >= 2): trials 1/2 (A wins the .93 expert but loses the tally 1-4) and trials 11/12 (the two best experts tie so TTB descends to f2 and picks one option, while the tally favors the other by 2). This metric is the proportion of choices on exactly those trials that agree with the tally winner.

Prediction under Tallying: with margin magnitude 2-3, softmax choice is near-deterministic for the tally winner for almost the whole beta range, so the score is (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*|M|)+eps/2, i.e. near 0.85-1.0. Prediction under TTB: exactly the complement, eps/2 + (1-eps)*(1-sigmoid(beta)), i.e. near 0-0.15. The expected mean gap is ~0.7-0.75 while per-subject variance is small (only lapse-rate spread plus binomial noise over 32 trials at extreme p), which is what Welch's test at N=25 needs. Restricting to |M| >= 2 avoids the weak M=1 cells where Tallying's own prediction is soft; excluding agreement and tie cells removes trials where the two theories predict the same thing and which would only dilute the contrast.

This is the overall adherence rate to the full-tally winner (the option that wins on strictly more features), pooled over the 96 trials of the design (every trial in this design has a non-zero tally margin, so no trial is dropped).

Why it separates the theories: LSNC's core commitment is that only a small, randomly drawn subset of cues (mean k between 1.5 and 3.5 of the 6 features) is ever inspected, that tied cues occupy sampling slots (tie dilution), and that each inspected comparison is mis-registered with probability nu = .12-.32. A small noisy sample frequently reverses or fails to recover the sign of the global margin, so LSNC's adherence is structurally CAPPED: exact enumeration for this design gives ~0.57-0.75 across the six cells, i.e. an aggregate near 0.65-0.68, and it cannot approach 1 for any admissible parameter setting. Tallying, in contrast, reads every feature and passes the exact margin (M = 1, 2 or 3 here, never 0) through a softmax; over the bulk of its inverse-temperature range the softmax is essentially deterministic, so its adherence sits near 1 - epsilon/2, i.e. roughly 0.85-0.90 on average and never structurally attenuated by the composition of the profile.

This is not trivially true of my theory: Tallying is perfectly free to produce low adherence (small beta, large epsilon), and LSNC is free to produce moderately high adherence (large k, small nu) - the metric measures a behavioural ceiling, not a theory label. The prediction that humans in a 6-cue, feedback-free, high-conflict task fall far short of margin-consistent responding (adherence well below 0.8 even at margin 3) is the substantive LSNC claim; Tallying, which by construction integrates all cues, has to attribute any such shortfall to a degenerate temperature that would then also flatten the margin gradient. The metric is a simple proportion over ~96 trials per subject, so its per-subject sampling noise is small (sd ~0.04-0.05), keeping the between-subject variance tight relative to the ~0.2 mean gap.

The single sharpest quantitative divergence between the two accounts is the ATTAINABLE LEVEL of adherence to the complete-profile tally winner on clearly discriminating pairs. Every trial in this design has a strict global tally winner with margin M = 2 or M = 4, and (by construction) the option favoured by the tally also wins the most valid cue, so the metric is not confounded by cue-order strategies.

Under softmax Tallying the decision variable is the FULL margin: P(winner) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*M) + eps/2. Since M >= 2 on every trial, sigmoid(beta*M) is already essentially at ceiling for most of the beta range, so adherence is pinned near 1 - eps/2, i.e. roughly 0.85-0.90 on average and, crucially, only weakly dispersed (its across-subject spread comes from the lapse parameter alone, since 48 + 48 trials wash out binomial noise).

Under LSNC the inspected subset averages ~2.5 of 8 cues and each comparison is mis-registered with prob nu ~ 0.2, so a large global margin is routinely reversed or diluted by tied cues occupying sampling slots. Exact enumeration for this design gives adherence ~0.60-0.66 at M=2 and ~0.69-0.75 at M=4, i.e. a pooled value around 0.66-0.70 that is CAPPED well below what full integration produces, and again tightly distributed across subjects because the parameter ranges (k in [1.5,3.5], nu in [0.12,0.32]) move it only a few points.

So the expected contrast is roughly 0.87 vs 0.68 with per-subject variances of order 0.005-0.008 in both cases, which at N=25 is a very large Welch t. This is not trivially true of Tallying: had subjects been strongly noise-limited, Tallying's own epsilon/beta would drag adherence down toward the LSNC band; the prediction that adherence sits high above the sample-limited ceiling is a substantive commitment of full-cue integration.

The design holds the win-count composition (nA,nB,nT) exactly fixed while flipping whether the highest-validity expert (0.94) sides with or against the count winner. LSNC (advocated) samples cues uniformly at random, so its predicted adherence depends only on (nA,nB,nT) and is mathematically invariant to which cues the winner owns: the coherent-minus-conflict adherence difference is exactly 0 for every parameter setting (k, nu, epsilon). CDCC gates confidence through the convex validity-weighted coherence term C, with kappa >= 0.4 by hypothesis, so it must show a large positive gap (~0.15, i.e. ~0.71 coherent vs ~0.56 conflict). Each subject supplies 48 coherent and 48 conflict trials, so the within-subject difference has SE ~0.10, giving a very tight per-subject estimate and a between-theory separation of many standard errors at N=25. Side mirrors within each cell cancel any side bias, and the coherence label is derived generically (winner owns the most valid discriminating cue), so no trial-index bookkeeping is required.

Two structurally signed contrasts are summed, each of which has an opposite (or null) sign under the two theories, so the composite separates them with a large mean gap while each component is estimated from 32/32 and 16/16 trials per subject (tight per-subject noise).

D1 = adherence(count-winner) on validity-COHERENT conflicting profiles minus adherence on validity-INCOHERENT profiles, with the (nA,nB,nT) composition held EXACTLY matched across the two sets by design (T1/T2 vs T3/T4 both (2,1,4); T5/T6 vs T7/T8 both (4,2,1)). LSNC samples cues uniformly and ignores validity entirely, so its predicted adherence depends only on (nA,nB,nT): D1 = 0 exactly, for every k, nu, epsilon. CDCC gates confidence by the convex validity-weighted coherence C, so D1 is strictly positive (~+0.11 to +0.17, larger for larger kappa) and cannot be turned off.

D2 = adherence on the UNANIMOUS-SPARSE profile (2 winning cues, 0 opposing, 5 tied) minus adherence on the UNANIMOUS-DENSE profile (4 winning cues, 0 opposing, 3 tied). For CDCC the dilution term S = M/D^gamma gives 2^(1-gamma) vs 4^(1-gamma) = (2^(1-gamma))^2, and since gamma > 1 the sparse profile ALWAYS yields the larger confidence: D2 >= 0 for every admissible parameter vector. For LSNC tied cues waste sampling slots, so the dense profile (4/7 informative slots) always beats the sparse one (2/7): D2 < 0 (~ -0.06 to -0.12) for every admissible parameter vector.

Hence the composite D1 + D2 is bounded below by 0 under CDCC (expected ~ +0.18) and is expected to be clearly negative under LSNC (~ -0.09), a gap of roughly 0.27 with per-subject variance dominated by binomial sampling over 96 trials (sd ~ 0.17), which gives a Welch t well above 4 at N=25. It is not trivially true for CDCC: a flat coherence effect or an ordering with dense > sparse on unanimous profiles would push the metric to zero/negative and falsify it.
